method.model: Inherited Codex runtime; exact model snapshot unavailable.
method.independence: Separate contexts and randomized individual case orders. Shared model family may share biases; these are not independent human judgments.
method.coverage: Four selected screenshot tiles per capture plus full CSS-visible document text. Five distinct candidates and current live homepage, desktop and 375px phone; supplied companion excluded. Links and interactions were not systematically exercised by judges.
method.shortlist_rule: Exploratory selection after individual scoring: choose the two pages with the most dimensions scoring at least 2 from both judges at both widths. Untangle the Problem clears 6/6; Check the Because clears 5/6. All gates remain in force; the shortlist is for comparison, not approval to launch.
method.order_limit: Opposite orders were assigned to different fresh contexts. Disagreement combines session variation and possible position effects; it cannot isolate causal order bias.
method.source_limit: The reference brief describes the skill and local records, not an exhaustive inventory of every prototype or integration. Absence from that brief does not establish that a capability is false. Judge factual flags require source review.
method.calibration: No human labels, real visitor responses, conversion data or inferential statistics.

recommendation:
Start human testing with Untangle the Problem. Both scoring contexts marked it as meeting all six criteria at desktop and phone widths, with no reported gates. It gives the clearest complete path from a concrete problem through the reasoning process to trying the skill under this contract.

Keep Check the Because as the explanatory alternative. Both scoring contexts praised its worked mechanism and presentation, but gave its next action 0/3: a usable route to trying or installing the skill was not established in the captured evidence. Resolve that gap before treating it as a product-trial landing page.

Make Work Add Up is another useful revision candidate: its clarity, mechanism, relevance and starting instructions scored strongly, while availability/guarantee wording and phone diagram readability need attention. This is a provisional choice for a visitor study, not evidence that any page will convert better.

Both comparison contexts preferred Untangle the Problem for clarity and next action, and Check the Because for accuracy, mechanism and phone presentation. They tied relevance and desktop presentation. All 12 criterion outcomes matched after mapping the reversed A/B labels; this consistency does not establish correctness.

correction.heading: The Untangle the Problem recommendation is withdrawn
correction.text:
On 19 October these results recommended starting human testing with Untangle the Problem, partly because both judges scored its next action 3/3. Its only install route is a Download the skill button that calls Claude's artifact runtime. On the public preview and in a fresh local capture, the button reports: “This view can’t save files. Open the page in Claude on the web or desktop to download the skill.” The judges read page text and screenshots and did not exercise controls, so they could not see this.

The review found three further limits. The 70/72 score agreement measures repeatability within one model family, not correctness. Five of six criteria repeated identically at both widths because both received the same full text. Most top scores sat at the ceiling of the 0–3 scale.

No replacement page is chosen. The evaluator now uses yes/no checklists, a scripted main-action check that judges cannot override, a first-screen reading task and seeded-defect checks; a new judged run is needed before recommending a page. The original recommendation stays below for the record.

YOUR GOAL
WHAT THE GOAL RESTS ON
TEST THIS FIRST
You have an ambitious goal, and you’re working hard toward it.

But progress is uneven:

GOAL

a breakthrough here,

weeks of nothing there.

Lately it feels stalled.

The natural response is to push harder.

You run
more
studies,
spend
more
on marketing,
or add
more
to the program.

It feels like solid ground.

That’s what makes it hard to see.

1
This is the one assumption that would change where you put your effort if it turned out to be wrong,
2
and that you can test quickly and cheaply.

UNDERNEATH

ONE SMALL TEST

You’ve been building support for a new explanation, study by study. But the results keep coming back suggestive rather than decisive,

and every study depends on an assumption you’ve never directly tested.

One focused experiment tells you whether to

keep building on the idea
or rethink it

before you invest another year.

A small paid pilot tells you whether to

spend on spreading the word,
or on changing what you sell and to whom.

The assumption underneath is that missing skills are what’s holding participants back.

A small trial with one employer shows whether

more training is the answer,
or whether the real gap is access, relationships, or something else entirely.

AN OPEN-SOURCE SKILL FOR CLAUDE CODE, CODEX AND OTHER AGENTS

Make your team's work add up to its goal.

Talk through a goal, a problem or a disagreement with your agent. The reason-commons skill records who said what, what you've agreed and what's still open, and it asks every change you make to name the reasoning it serves.

$ npx skills add life-itself/reasoncommons -s reason-commons
COPY
Try it without installing
Read the skill on GitHub ↗

MIT licensed · No account or app · Your reasoning lives in a YAML file you own

Why does PR #142 exist?
reason-commons.yaml
[A] CURRENT REALITY · UNDESIRABLE EFFECT
Customers often wait more than three days for quotes
Bob · accepted by Alice
↑ contributes to
[A] CURRENT REALITY · CAUSE
Only the pricing lead can approve discounts
Alice · accepted by Alice

✓

Read it from the bottom up. The pull request names the change it puts into practice, and the change traces back to the problem it is meant to fix.

THE PROBLEM

The plan says one thing. The work does another.

A group agrees on what it's trying to do. Then the real reasoning happens in calls, chats and pull requests, and very little of it gets written back. After a few weeks it's hard to say which goal a piece of work was for.

01
A pull request merges, and nobody can say which goal it served.
02
A call reaches agreement. A week later it's largely forgotten.
03
An objection is raised, lost, and raised again next month.

Goal trees, cause-and-effect trees and conflict clouds were built for problems like this. They come from the Logical Thinking Process, part of Eliyahu Goldratt's Theory of Constraints, and they have been in use for forty years. They rarely survive in a busy team, because someone has to stop working to keep them current. An agent can now keep the trees current while the people keep talking.

HOW A SESSION GOES

One conversation, start to finish

Alice and Bob want to know why customer quotes keep going out late. Scroll through their session. The tree beside it is what the skill saves to reason-commons.yaml after each turn.

reason-commons.yaml · current_reality

Bob

01
It starts from what you know

No template and no method to learn first. It asks for the one thing it needs now, and one participant is enough to begin.

ALICE

Use the reason-commons skill to help us work out why customer quotes are late. I'm Alice; Bob's here too.

AGENT · REASON-COMMONS

Next: start with one recent quote that went out late.

Why: nothing is recorded yet, and a real case gives us something concrete to explain.

Focus: late customer quotes · Driver: Alice · Other participants: Bob

What happened between the request and the quote going out?

02
It writes things down as you talk

Each contribution becomes one clear statement with the contributor's name on it. New reasoning starts as proposed, and the agent marks its own suggestions as its own.

BOB

Customers often wait more than three days. Usually sales is sitting on pricing approval.

AGENT · REASON-COMMONS

Saved: two statements from Bob, both proposed: customers often wait more than three days for quotes, and sales often waits for pricing approval, linked as a possible cause.

Next: check whether approval is enough on its own.

Why: if late quotes need two conditions together, removing either one might be enough.

Does waiting for approval always make a quote late, or only when something else is true too?

03
It keeps joint causes joint

Conditions that only matter together meet at an AND, so neither is treated as enough on its own. When a piece of reasoning holds together, it offers it for review instead of piling on more.

ALICE

And only our pricing lead can approve discounts, so everything waits for her.

AGENT · REASON-COMMONS

Saved: one statement from Alice, proposed: only the pricing lead can approve discounts. I've joined it to Bob's cause at an AND, because the delay comes from both together.

The branch now holds together: one effect and two causes acting jointly.

You can accept it for now, or revise it.

04
Accepted means “for now”

Only an explicit yes changes the standing. Silence, moving on or viewing the tree never counts. Each accepted change saves a numbered snapshot and redraws two diagrams: the full tree and the latest change.

ALICE

That's right. Accept it for now.

AGENT · REASON-COMMONS

Saved: accepted for now: the three statements and the joint link. That means we're willing to build on it, not that it's proven. Snapshot 1 is saved and the diagrams are updated.

Next: collect a few more late quotes.

Why: a handful of cases will show whether approval explains most of them.

What else has made a quote late recently?

05
Disagreement stays on the record

An objection stays attached to the item it challenges, with the name of whoever raised it, until it's resolved. Unfinished reasoning waits in a backlog instead of getting lost.

BOB

I'm not convinced approval is the main thing. Half our late quotes are custom configurations.

AGENT · REASON-COMMONS

Saved: Bob's objection, kept on the approval link, which is now disputed. The three statements stay accepted. His point is also recorded as a proposed cause: many late quotes involve custom configurations.

Next: count custom configurations among the last ten late quotes.

Why: the count tells us which cause to work on first.

Bob, can you pull those ten quotes?

START WHEREVER YOU ARE

You can begin with a goal, a problem, a disagreement, a proposed change, an obstacle or a list of actions. The skill chooses the kind of tree that fits, so nobody needs to learn the method first.

FOR WORK IN A REPOSITORY

No change without a reason

When the working file lives in your repository, the skill connects each change to the reasoning behind it.

1
You ask for a change, even just “fix it”.
It replies with a change proposal: the reasoning it serves, the tree updates it will make, the files it will touch and how it will be checked.
2
Nothing is edited until you type yes.
Your reply is saved word for word, with the proposal's version, its scope, the approved files and the time.
3
The pull request carries the trace.
Its description shows the reasoning changes as a diagram, and a check fails the PR if the listed tree updates don't match the YAML.

Approving the work doesn't endorse the reasoning. Claims stay proposed until someone accepts them, and merging a pull request doesn't change that.

We run the Reason Commons repository this way. The pull request that introduced the rule had to follow it, and its tree check passed.

INSTALL

Start in a minute

Free and open source under the MIT licence. It works in Claude Code, Codex and other agents that support SKILL.md skills.

1
Install the skill
npx skills add life-itself/reasoncommons -s reason-commons
COPY

It asks which agents to install into. To install for one agent in every project, add -a claude-code -g and swap in the agent you use.

2
Start a conversation
Use the reason-commons skill to help me think through why customer quotes are late. My name is Alice. Keep the working state in reason-commons.yaml.
COPY

Open your agent in the folder where the working state should live, then swap in your own topic and name.

3
Pick it up later
Use the reason-commons skill and resume from reason-commons.yaml. Show me the most useful unfinished reasoning to work on next.
COPY

For a group, name people as they contribute. If speaker labels come from a transcript, pass those in; the skill never guesses who spoke.

Rather not install anything?
Print the skill as a ready-to-paste prompt. An installed copy includes the helper scripts, so installing is the better option.
npx skills use life-itself/reasoncommons@reason-commons
COPY
What it leaves behind

Everything stays in files next to your work. The YAML is the source of truth; the diagrams are drawn from it after each accepted change.

reason-commons.yaml
trees, contributors, backlog
.reason-commons/history/000001.yaml
one snapshot per accepted change
.reason-commons/diagrams/current/
the full accepted tree
.reason-commons/diagrams/changes/
the latest accepted change

The diagram helper needs Python with PyYAML. It draws the SVG itself, with no Graphviz or JavaScript renderer.

A latest-change view drawn by the helper for the skill's remote-work test example: revised wording in amber, the removed link dashed red, unchanged neighbours in grey.

QUESTIONS

Fair questions
Do we need to know the Logical Thinking Process?

No. Start with whatever you have: a goal, a problem, a disagreement, a proposed change, an obstacle or a list of actions. The skill chooses the kind of tree that fits and never asks you to learn its name.

Does “accepted” mean it's true?

No. Accepted means the group is willing to build on it for now. Anyone can challenge it later, and the objection is kept with their name until it's resolved.

Can a whole group use it?

Yes. Name people as they contribute, or pass in speaker labels from a transcript. Each idea stays attributed to whoever had it, and the skill never guesses who spoke.

Where does our reasoning live?

In a YAML file in your folder or repository, with snapshots and diagrams beside it. There's no account and no server. You can read it, diff it and commit it like any other file.

Won't the approval step slow small changes down?

Somewhat. Every requested change gets a proposal first, even a small fix. We've written down the risk that this tempts people to cite reasoning loosely, and we're watching for it.

Is it finished?

No. It's early and changes most weeks; the changelog shows what's new. Its YAML is separate from the Reason Commons app, and the ltp-project skill is still the way to draft an app import file.

PASS IT ON

Know a team whose work keeps drifting?

Send them this. It has everything they need to try it.

Try the Reason Commons skill to think through a goal, problem, conflict or plan together. Install it with npx skills add life-itself/reasoncommons -s reason-commons, then ask your agent: "Use the reason-commons skill to help me think through [topic]. My name is [name]." The agent keeps unfinished reasoning in a backlog and turns explicitly accepted reasoning into full and latest-change diagrams. More: https://reasoncommons.com/skills

Fair questions
Do we need to know the Logical Thinking Process?

No. Start with whatever you have: a goal, a problem, a disagreement, a proposed change, an obstacle or a list of actions. The skill chooses the kind of tree that fits and never asks you to learn its name.

Guided reasoning, in plain words

Untangle the problem you keep coming back to.

Reason Commons is an AI facilitator for recurring problems, stuck decisions and plans you aren’t sure about. It asks one useful question at a time, maps your reasoning as you answer, and keeps a record of what you’ve agreed, what’s disputed and what still needs testing.

Try it on your problem

Watch a session unfold

Runs inside Claude or Codex
No method to learn first
Works alone or with a team

Focus: why releases slip · Driver: Maya · Other participants: Jon

MAYA

Our releases keep slipping. Usually by about two weeks, sometimes more.

P
PROPOSED
PROBLEM
Maya
Releases usually slip by about two weeks, sometimes more.

Recorded as proposed, with her qualifiers kept

REASON COMMONS

NEXT: Think of the last release that slipped. What was the first thing that didn’t happen when you expected it to?

WHY: One real case shows where the delay starts, before anyone guesses at causes.

One question, with the reason for asking it

The pattern

You’ve been here before.

Retro notes · third time this quarter

The fix that didn’t stick

The same issue is back in the retro. Every fix made sense when you made it. None of them reached whatever keeps causing it.

Decision log · open for six weeks

The argument on repeat

Two people you trust keep making the same points. Each is right about something. Six weeks on, the decision still isn’t made.

Plan review · approved

The plan everyone nodded at

It sounded convincing in the meeting. Nobody traced how the first step leads to the result, or what it might break along the way.

Six months later

The reason nobody kept

Someone asks why you chose this. The people who knew have moved on, and the thread that explained it is buried somewhere.

These have the same root. The reasoning underneath stays in people’s heads.

What leads to what, what each side needs, what has to be true for the plan to work. Nobody lays it out, so nobody tests it. Nobody records it, so every discussion starts again from the beginning.

Why AI hasn’t fixed it

Answers are abundant. Reasoning isn’t.

Ask a general-purpose AI and you’ll get a confident, well-organised answer in seconds. It reads well. It’s also built from the model’s assumptions about situations like yours, its guesses sit next to your facts without a label, and nothing records which parts you actually accept. Next week you’re back with the same problem and a slightly different answer.

A TYPICAL GENERIC ANSWER · ILLUSTRATIVE

Release delays often come from scope creep, testing bottlenecks or optimistic estimates. Common fixes:

Freeze scope earlier in each cycle
Automate regression testing
Ship unfinished work behind feature flags
Track cycle time to find the bottleneck

Want a rollout plan for any of these?

Sensible fixes, drawn from teams in general. Nothing here checks what is actually happening on yours, or keeps track of what you agree with.

PROPOSED
PROBLEM
You

NEXT: Has a recent release shipped on time? If so, what was different about it?

WHY: A release that didn’t slip is the quickest way to test any explanation you already have.

One question about your situation. The answer goes into a map you can test, agree on and keep.

Why this exists

Clear thinking shouldn’t be a privilege.

The methods behind Reason Commons come from Eli Goldratt’s Theory of Constraints and H. William Dettmer’s Logical Thinking Process. Since the 1990s they’ve mostly been taught in workshops and consultancies, to people with the time and budget to learn them.

Today it’s a skill you add to Claude or Codex.

Good reasoning belongs to everyone.

A different way to work

Make the reasoning itself the thing you work on.

Reason Commons turns a conversation into reasoning you can see, test and keep. You talk the way you normally would. The structure builds up underneath.

Lay it out

What you say becomes clear, single statements joined by the connections you describe. Words like “usually” and “might” stay in.

Test it

Connections get examined one question at a time. Why would this lead to that? What else has to be true? Is it necessary, or only helpful?

Agree on it out loud

Everything starts as proposed, your own claims included. Nothing becomes accepted until someone says so, and objections stay on the record with their author.

Keep it

The reasoning is saved to a plain file you own, with a numbered snapshot whenever accepted reasoning changes. Pick it up next week where you stopped.

How agreement works

Everything starts in pencil.

Each statement and connection carries a standing, shown by its border as well as its label, so you can always tell what’s settled for now and what isn’t.

P
PROPOSED · CAUSE
Jon

A

See it work

Watch a session take shape.

Releases keep slipping
2 people
Hire now or wait?
1 person

Our releases keep slipping. Usually by about two weeks, sometimes more.

How a session works

Four moves, at your pace.
Bring what you already know

A symptom, a stalemate, a plan or a goal. There’s no template to fill in. The structure is chosen from what you say.

Answer one question at a time

Each turn ends with one focused question and the reason for asking it. Take a different direction whenever you like.

Watch it firm up

Your answers become statements and connections, proposed until you accept them. Untested links and open objections go on a short list of work.

Leave with something to act on

What you agree on, what’s disputed and the next test worth running, saved so you can pick it up again.

Where it helps

Bring it the thing you’re stuck on.

Four common starting points. Copy a prompt to use with the skill, or adapt it to your situation.

A recurring problem

Why does this keep happening?

START WITH

Our releases keep slipping, usually by about two weeks. Help me work out why before we change anything else.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
Think of the last time it happened. What was the first thing that didn’t go as expected?
YOU LEAVE WITH
The causes you’ve tested, the ones you accept for now, and the check that would change your mind.

A stuck disagreement

Why do we keep having this argument?

START WITH

My co-founder wants to hire now and I want to wait until revenue covers it. We’ve argued for a month. Help me see what each of us actually needs.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
What do you think your co-founder is trying to protect by hiring now?
YOU LEAVE WITH
Both positions, the need behind each, the assumption that makes them clash, and an option worth testing.

A change you’re about to make

Will this plan actually work?

START WITH

We’re moving customer support to tickets only. Help me check whether it will really cut response times, and what it could make worse.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
If it works exactly as you hope, what would a customer notice first?
YOU LEAVE WITH
How the change should produce the result, what else has to hold, and the side effects to guard against.

A goal that’s still fuzzy

What does good look like here?

START WITH

I want our onboarding to be better, but I can’t say what better means. Help me pin down the goal and what it depends on.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
Picture a new customer’s first week once onboarding works the way you want. What’s different for them?
YOU LEAVE WITH
A clear goal, the few conditions it depends on, and a check on each one that asks whether you could reach the goal without it.

Opening questions are examples of how the skill tends to start. Your session follows what you actually say.

What’s different

What it does that a plain chat doesn’t.

The skill follows facilitation rules written into it. These are the ones you’ll notice first.

It asks before it assumes

If your reasoning depends on something that’s missing, it helps you establish it instead of filling the gap itself.

Your qualifiers survive

“Sometimes” stays “sometimes”. A hunch isn’t quietly rounded up into a fact when it’s written down.

Its own ideas are labelled

When the AI suggests a cause or a connection, it says so, and the file records it as the AI’s, separate from what people said.

Silence isn’t agreement

Moving on, viewing the map or saying nothing never counts as acceptance. Only an explicit yes does.

Objections stay attached

A challenged claim is marked disputed, with the objection and who raised it, until you resolve it.

It finishes before it widens

Once there’s enough material, it works through untested links and open questions before asking you for more.

How it compares with what you’d use today
How it compares with what you’d use today
QUESTION
	ASKING A GENERAL AI	WHITEBOARD OR DIAGRAM TOOL	MEETING AND NOTES	REASON COMMONS
You come away with	An answer to evaluate	A diagram	Decisions and notes	Your reasoning, laid out and tested
Whose thinking it is	The model’s, blended with yours	The group’s, as drawn	The group’s, as remembered	Yours, with the AI’s suggestions recorded as its own
What counts as agreed	Not tracked	Not tracked	Whatever the notes say, if someone writes them	Explicit: proposed, accepted for now or disputed
How claims get tested	When you ask it to	As the group discusses	When someone pushes back	Built into each session, one connection at a time
What’s left a week later	A chat history	A picture, without the reasons	Notes, if someone took them	A file with history and who said what, kept wherever you keep the file

Under the hood

A careful method you don’t have to learn first.

Reason Commons draws on the Logical Thinking Process, a set of reasoning structures from the Theory of Constraints for mapping causes, resolving conflicts, checking proposed changes, clearing obstacles and sequencing action. The structures are thorough, and they usually take training to use well. You don’t need to know them to start. The skill picks the structure from what you bring, and its diagrams name each structure when you want to look closer.

Plain-text memory
One YAML file holds the participants, statements, connections, standing and open work.
History you can trust
Whenever accepted reasoning changes, the helper saves a numbered snapshot that is never edited afterwards.
Views from the file
Diagrams are generated from the saved reasoning, one standing at a time, with joint causes shown as AND.
Works where you do
Diagrams render in apps that support them and fall back to readable text where they don’t.
reason-commons.yaml · excerpt from the example session
schema_version: 1
links:
  - id: l3
    from: [c1, c2]            # two causes acting together
    to: e1
    relation: contributes_to
    status: accepted
    accepted_by: [maya, jon]
    contributions:
      - {by: assistant, attribution: assistant, mode: text}
  - id: l1
    from: [c1]
    to: e1
    relation: contributes_to
    status: disputed
    contributions:
      - {by: maya, attribution: explicit, mode: text}
    challenges:
      - {text: Late QA on its own didn't cause a slip in March., by: jon}

For teams that build with AI agents

Every change traced to the reasoning it serves.

When an AI agent edits your code, the reason for each change is easy to lose. Inside a repository, the skill has the agent show a change proposal before it edits anything: the reasoning the change serves, the files it will touch and how the result will be checked. The agent waits for your typed acceptance, which is recorded with your exact words, the scope and the time. A pull-request check then confirms that every changed file and reasoning update is covered by an acceptance on record.

EXAMPLE, ABBREVIATED
The real proposal also includes a diagram of the tree updates.

1
The agent proposes

Type: Change proposal

Proposal: release-scope-freeze · revision 1

Change: Add a scope-freeze date to the release checklist.

Files: docs/release-checklist.md, reason-commons.yaml

Reasoning served: Future Reality · Injection · Proposed · f1: Freeze scope two weeks before QA on the next release. It addresses e1, the release slips.

Tree updates (proposed): Add Transition · Action · Proposed · t1: Add a scope-freeze date to the release checklist. Implements f1.

Validation: The next release records a freeze date, and its ship date is compared with the prediction in f2. One release can support the explanation but can’t prove it.

Status: Awaiting your typed acceptance before implementation, because changes to project files need a recorded approval. Reply to accept this version, or say what to change.

“Injection” is the method’s word for a change you propose. A transition action is one step that puts it in place.

2
You accept, in your own words
Maya: Yes, accept release-scope-freeze
revision 1.

change_acceptances:
  - proposal_ref: release-scope-freeze
    proposal_revision: 1
    by: maya
    recorded_at: '2026-10-18T09:12:00Z'
    timezone: Europe/Berlin
    mode: text
    source: conversation
    source_text: Yes, accept
      release-scope-freeze revision 1.
    scope: Add a scope-freeze date to
      the release checklist, and the
      proposed action t1.
    node_ids: [t1]
    link_ids: []
    approved_paths:
      [docs/release-checklist.md,
       reason-commons.yaml]

The receipt keeps who accepted, what they typed, the scope, the files and when it was recorded. Approving the work doesn’t count as agreeing with the reasoning.

3
The pull request is checked
$ check_pr_trees.py reason-commons.yaml --base origin/main --body-file pr.md

Tree check passed: serves 1 existing item(s); 1 tree update(s) match the YAML; recorded acceptances cover 2 changed file(s).

The check fails if a changed file or reasoning update isn’t covered by an acceptance on record, or if an earlier receipt was altered. It verifies coverage. It can’t prove who typed an acceptance or that the code does what was approved, so people still review the work.

Works in Claude Code and Codex. Comes with a pull-request template and a GitHub Actions workflow you can add to your repository once you point its paths at your copy of the skill.

Get started

Try it on your problem.

Start a short live session right here, or add the full skill to the assistant you already use.

LIVE PREVIEW

Runs on your own Claude account. Nothing is saved.

The live preview isn’t available here.

It needs Claude, signed in, and this view can’t reach it.

You can still step through the scripted sessions above, or get the skill below and paste your problem into Claude.

Watch the scripted session

The full skill

Keep going, and keep the reasoning.

The full skill saves your reasoning to a file, keeps its history and works with a whole team.

Download the skill
.zip · 72 KB

Claude
Claude Code
Codex
Download the skill.
In Claude, open Customize, then Skills, and add the .zip file.
Check that code execution is turned on. The skill uses it to save your reasoning.
Start a new chat and describe your problem, or paste one of the prompts above.

Your first ten minutes

01
It asks what’s going on, in your words. If you ask what to do, it recommends one next step and shows the reasoning behind it.
02
Within a few answers you’ll see your first piece of reasoning, and you can accept it for now or revise it.
03
It names one next step each turn and says why. You can always go a different way.

Where this could go

A commons for reasoning.

Today Reason Commons is a skill you add to the AI assistant you already use. The idea underneath is bigger. Reasoning can become a shared resource that people build together, test in the open and keep, so decisions stay connected to the thinking behind them.

Available today
IN THE SKILL
Guided sessions for one person or a group, in Claude and Codex
Proposed, accepted-for-now and disputed standing, with who said what
A saved reasoning file with numbered history and generated diagrams
Change proposals, recorded approvals and pull-request checks for code
Not built yet
POSSIBLE NEXT STEPS
Shared spaces where a team adds to the same reasoning at the same time
A searchable record of why past decisions were made
Automatic reminders to compare a plan’s predictions with what actually happened
Open commons where communities reason through contested questions in public

The “Not built yet” column describes directions the approach points toward. None of it is available today.

Questions

Before you try it.
Do I need to know the method?

No. Describe the situation in your own words and the skill chooses the structure. Its diagrams use the method’s names, so you’ll pick them up if you want to.

Isn’t this slower than just asking for an answer?

Answer one question at a time and you’ll see it laid out in your own words, with the next thing worth testing.

Try it on your problem

Download the skill

Good reasoning belongs to everyone.

What you say becomes clear, single statements joined by the connections you describe. Words like “usually” and “might” stay in.

Test it

Connections get examined one question at a time. Why would this lead to that? What else has to be true? Is it necessary, or only helpful?

Agree on it out loud

Everything starts as proposed, your own claims included. Nothing becomes accepted until someone says so, and objections stay on the record with their author.

Keep it

The reasoning is saved to a plain file you own, with a numbered snapshot whenever accepted reasoning changes. Pick it up next week where you stopped.

How agreement works

Everything starts in pencil.

Each statement and connection carries a standing, shown by its border as well as its label, so you can always tell what’s settled for now and what isn’t.

Jon
Scope often changes late in the sprint.

Proposed. Captured but not yet agreed. Your own statements start here too.

A
ACCEPTED · PROBLEM
Maya

Accepted for now by Maya and Jon

Accepted for now. Someone said they’re willing to build on it. It isn’t a claim of proof, and it can be reopened.

D
DISPUTED · CAUSE
Maya

Objection (Jon): March shipped on time even though QA started late.

Disputed. Someone objected. The objection and its author stay attached until it’s resolved.

How a session works

Four moves, at your pace.
Bring what you already know

A symptom, a stalemate, a plan or a goal. There’s no template to fill in. The structure is chosen from what you say.

Answer one question at a time

Each turn ends with one focused question and the reason for asking it. Take a different direction whenever you like.

Watch it firm up

Your answers become statements and connections, proposed until you accept them. Untested links and open objections go on a short list of work.

Leave with something to act on

What you agree on, what’s disputed and the next test worth running, saved so you can pick it up again.

Where it helps

Bring it the thing you’re stuck on.

Four common starting points. Copy a prompt to use with the skill, or adapt it to your situation.

A recurring problem

Why does this keep happening?

START WITH

Our releases keep slipping, usually by about two weeks. Help me work out why before we change anything else.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
Think of the last time it happened. What was the first thing that didn’t go as expected?
YOU LEAVE WITH
The causes you’ve tested, the ones you accept for now, and the check that would change your mind.

A stuck disagreement

Why do we keep having this argument?

START WITH

My co-founder wants to hire now and I want to wait until revenue covers it. We’ve argued for a month. Help me see what each of us actually needs.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
What do you think your co-founder is trying to protect by hiring now?
YOU LEAVE WITH
Both positions, the need behind each, the assumption that makes them clash, and an option worth testing.

A change you’re about to make

Will this plan actually work?

START WITH

We’re moving customer support to tickets only. Help me check whether it will really cut response times, and what it could make worse.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
If it works exactly as you hope, what would a customer notice first?
YOU LEAVE WITH
How the change should produce the result, what else has to hold, and the side effects to guard against.

A goal that’s still fuzzy

What does good look like here?

START WITH

I want our onboarding to be better, but I can’t say what better means. Help me pin down the goal and what it depends on.

Copy prompt
IT MIGHT OPEN WITH
Picture a new customer’s first week once onboarding works the way you want. What’s different for them?
YOU LEAVE WITH
A clear goal, the few conditions it depends on, and a check on each one that asks whether you could reach the goal without it.

Opening questions are examples of how the skill tends to start. Your session follows what you actually say.

What’s different

What it does that a plain chat doesn’t.

The skill follows facilitation rules written into it. These are the ones you’ll notice first.

It asks before it assumes

If your reasoning depends on something that’s missing, it helps you establish it instead of filling the gap itself.

Your qualifiers survive

“Sometimes” stays “sometimes”. A hunch isn’t quietly rounded up into a fact when it’s written down.

Its own ideas are labelled

When the AI suggests a cause or a connection, it says so, and the file records it as the AI’s, separate from what people said.

Silence isn’t agreement

Moving on, viewing the map or saying nothing never counts as acceptance. Only an explicit yes does.

Objections stay attached

A challenged claim is marked disputed, with the objection and who raised it, until you resolve it.

It finishes before it widens

Once there’s enough material, it works through untested links and open questions before asking you for more.

How it compares with what you’d use today

Scroll sideways for Reason Commons →

How it compares with what you’d use today
QUESTION
	ASKING A GENERAL AI	WHITEBOARD OR DIAGRAM TOOL	MEETING AND NOTES	REASON COMMONS
You come away with	An answer to evaluate	A diagram	Decisions and notes	Your reasoning, laid out and tested
Whose thinking it is	The model’s, blended with yours	The group’s, as drawn	The group’s, as remembered	Yours, with the AI’s suggestions recorded as its own
What counts as agreed	Not tracked	Not tracked	Whatever the notes say, if someone writes them	Explicit: proposed, accepted for now or disputed
How claims get tested	When you ask it to	As the group discusses	When someone pushes back	Built into each session, one connection at a time
What’s left a week later	A chat history	A picture, without the reasons	Notes, if someone took them	A file with history and who said what, kept wherever you keep the file

Under the hood

A careful method you don’t have to learn first.

Reason Commons draws on the Logical Thinking Process, a set of reasoning structures from the Theory of Constraints for mapping causes, resolving conflicts, checking proposed changes, clearing obstacles and sequencing action. The structures are thorough, and they usually take training to use well. You don’t need to know them to start. The skill picks the structure from what you bring, and its diagrams name each structure when you want to look closer.

Plain-text memory
One YAML file holds the participants, statements, connections, standing and open work.
History you can trust
Whenever accepted reasoning changes, the helper saves a numbered snapshot that is never edited afterwards.
Views from the file
Diagrams are generated from the saved reasoning, one standing at a time, with joint causes shown as AND.
Works where you do
Diagrams render in apps that support them and fall back to readable text where they don’t.

Every change traced to the reasoning it serves.

When an AI agent edits your code, the reason for each change is easy to lose. Inside a repository, the skill has the agent show a change proposal before it edits anything: the reasoning the change serves, the files it will touch and how the result will be checked. Reason Commons
Join

A RENAISSANCE OF COMMON SENSE

What if the world isn’t short of good ideas?

What if we’re just rather bad at thinking together?

A
B
C
D
your view
my view
the
commons
Fig. I — Two views, one commons.
We’ve put people on the Moon.
We’ve taught machines to write poetry.
We’ve invented refrigerators that can connect to the internet.
Yet we still have meetings about why we’re having so many meetings.

Something has gone slightly wrong.

Not with our intelligence.

With how we use it.

Welcome to Reason Commons.

A place to rediscover the surprisingly radical art of making sense.

Together.

Come Think With Us

We’ve made incredible progress in artificial intelligence.

Perhaps it’s time we made some progress in collective intelligence.

I.
THE PROBLEM

We’ve become extraordinarily good at solving the wrong problems.

Every year, organisations spend billions becoming more efficient.

They optimise departments, measure performance, introduce systems, hire consultants and develop elaborate strategies.

And somehow, the problems remain.

Sometimes they become more expensive.

This isn’t necessarily because people are foolish.

Quite the opposite.

It’s often because intelligent people are very good at making individually sensible decisions that produce collectively ridiculous outcomes.

EACH PART

A hospital can run every department efficiently

THE WHOLE

while patients wait for hours.

EACH PART

A company can meet every performance target

THE WHOLE

while disappointing its customers.

EACH PART

A school can improve its examination results

THE WHOLE

while diminishing its pupils’ curiosity.

It’s entirely possible for everyone to be doing their best while the system gets worse.

Which suggests an intriguing possibility.

Perhaps the problem isn’t the people.

Perhaps it’s the way we’re thinking about the problem.

A THIRTY-SECOND EXPERIMENT

You run a small hospital. You can give one department 50% more capacity. Which one?

Every patient passes through all five departments, in order.

THE WHOLE HOSPITAL TREATS

10
patients an hour

1
Reception
30 an hour
2
Triage
24 an hour
3
Doctors
10 an hour
4
Tests
18 an hour
5
Discharge
22 an hour

Pick a department to give it 50% more capacity.

II.
THE BIG IDEA

Common sense isn’t nearly as common as it ought to be.

Not because people lack it.

But because we’ve made thinking unnecessarily complicated.

We’ve professionalised it.
Departmentalised it.
Wrapped it in impressive terminology.
Put it behind expensive qualifications.
And occasionally turned rather obvious truths into diagrams requiring six hours of explanation.
Fig. II — A rather obvious truth, professionally explained.

Consider this:

If you want to improve something, it helps to understand what’s stopping it from improving.

Not exactly rocket science.

Yet remarkably little of what we call improvement begins there.

Instead, we often improve whatever is easiest to measure, most politically convenient, or currently fashionable.

We make the parts better and hope the whole improves.

It frequently doesn’t.

Reason Commons begins with a different idea.

Before trying to make things better, let’s make better sense of things.

III.
A DIFFERENT KIND OF RENAISSANCE

The Renaissance didn’t invent human intelligence.

It changed what people believed they could do with it.

What if we could do that again?

Not with painting or architecture.

With reasoning.

i.
Imagine if understanding cause and effect became as natural as reading.
ii.
If questioning an assumption was regarded as a contribution rather than a challenge to authority.
iii.
If disagreement became an opportunity to discover something neither person had previously considered.
iv.
If children learned to resolve apparent contradictions before learning to defend positions.
v.
If organisations spent less time managing symptoms and more time understanding what produces them.
vi.
And if ordinary people discovered that many seemingly impossible problems are not impossible at all.

They’re simply being viewed through assumptions nobody has thought to question.

That would be quite a renaissance.

And it wouldn’t require everyone to become a genius.

Just a little more curious.

IV.
WHY A COMMONS?

Some things become more valuable when we share them.

A sandwich isn’t one of them.

A good idea is.

A SANDWICH

If I give you half my sandwich, I have less sandwich.

A GOOD IDEA

me
you
If I help you understand something, we may both end up understanding more.

Reasoning has this wonderful property.

It can become richer through sharing.

Yet much of the world’s useful thinking remains trapped inside disciplines, professions, organisations and methodologies.

Economists
have their language.
Psychologists
have theirs.
Engineers
have another.
Management consultants
appear to have several thousand.

Meanwhile, the rest of us are expected to get on with life.

Reason Commons exists to make useful reasoning more accessible, more social and more contagious.

Not as another proprietary system.

But as something we can cultivate together.

A commons.

A shared space for better questions, better explanations and better ways forward.

V.
THE METHOD BEHIND THE MADNESS

It turns out that common sense benefits from a little discipline.

Thinking clearly isn’t simply a matter of trusting your instincts.

Our instincts are wonderful.

They’re also occasionally spectacularly wrong.

Which is why Reason Commons draws inspiration from the Theory of Constraints and its tradition of examining cause and effect, questioning assumptions and resolving conflicts.

Its starting insight is deceptively simple.

In any system, a surprisingly small number of things often determine what the whole system can achieve.

1
Find what matters most.
2
Understand why it matters.
3
Change what needs changing.
4
Then see what happens.

Of course, real life is rarely quite that tidy.

People disagree.
Objectives conflict.
Unintended consequences appear.
Yesterday’s solution becomes tomorrow’s problem.

That’s why we need more than slogans.

We need ways to test our explanations against reality.
Ways to distinguish symptoms from causes.
Ways to uncover the assumptions keeping a conflict alive.
And ways to make progress without requiring everyone to agree about everything first.

We don’t believe everyone needs to learn the vocabulary of the Theory of Constraints.

We believe more people could benefit from experiencing what its thinking tools make possible.

The tools matter. But what people can accomplish with them matters more.

VI.

Five questions that could change quite a lot

Better thinking often begins with surprisingly ordinary questions.

1
What are we actually trying to achieve?

An embarrassingly useful question, especially in organisations that have become extremely busy.

2
What’s stopping us?

Not everything that’s wrong. The things that genuinely limit progress.

3
Why does that happen?

And why does that happen? Keep going until the explanation becomes useful.

4
What are we assuming?

Some of our most formidable obstacles turn out to be beliefs masquerading as facts.

5
What would change our minds?

Because being certain feels wonderful, but discovering you were mistaken can be considerably more valuable.

None of these questions requires a PhD.

They do, however, require something that can be remarkably difficult to find.

The willingness to think together.

Explore the Questions

VII.

A movement for people who suspect there must be a better way

You don’t have to be an expert.

In fact, it may help if you aren’t.

Reason Commons is for people who have ever looked at an established way of doing things and thought:

Surely this can’t be the best we can do?

EDUCATORS
It’s for educators who want children to think rather than merely repeat.
LEADERS
For leaders who suspect their organisations contain more untapped intelligence than their consultants.
ENTREPRENEURS
For entrepreneurs who know the obvious solution is not always the right one.
COMMUNITIES
For communities tired of arguments that generate heat but no light.
PRACTITIONERS
For practitioners who have discovered powerful thinking tools and wonder why more people haven’t encountered them.
ANYONE
And for anyone who believes that disagreement needn’t end in division.
You don’t need permission.
You don’t need a qualification.
You don’t even need to agree with us.

Actually, disagreement could be rather useful.

You just need to be willing to question what seems obvious.

Join the Commons

VIII.

What happens here?

Less intellectual theatre. More useful thinking.

Explore

Discover deceptively simple ideas that change how you see problems.

Practise

Learn to use questions, reasoning tools and experiments on situations that actually matter to you.

Gather

Bring people together around shared challenges, even when they start with different opinions.

Contribute

Share questions, discoveries, stories, tools and explanations that others can learn from.

Spread

Help make better reasoning an everyday human capability, rather than a specialist occupation.

The ambition isn’t to build an audience that admires good thinking.

It’s to build a commons in which people practise it.

IX.
OUR MANIFESTO

We have enough people trying to sound clever.

We could do with more people trying to understand.

We believe a question can be more valuable than an answer.

That disagreement is not necessarily a sign of stupidity.
That complexity is sometimes real, but sometimes merely a symptom of poor explanation.
That local improvements can make the whole worse.
That incentives matter.
That assumptions deserve examination.
That evidence matters more than elegance.
That the purpose of reasoning is not to win arguments, but to make progress.
And that no one has a monopoly on common sense.

Especially us.

Reason Commons is not a movement to tell the world what to think.

It’s a movement to help us think better together.

X.
THE INVITATION

The world probably doesn’t need another methodology.

It might, however, benefit from a renaissance.

A renaissance in curiosity.
In cause and effect.
In intellectual humility.
In the rather unfashionable belief that people with different perspectives can work together to discover something neither could see alone.
And in the possibility that many of our most frustrating problems might become easier to solve once we stop treating their symptoms as their causes.

It begins with a question.

Not a course.
Not a certification.
Not a 147-slide presentation.

Just a question.

What if there’s a better way to think about this?

Welcome to Reason Commons.

A Renaissance of Common Sense.

Join the Renaissance

Bring your curiosity. Leave your certainty at the door.

Which is why Reason Commons draws inspiration from the Theory of Constraints and its tradition of examining cause and effect, questioning assumptions and resolving conflicts.

Its starting insight is deceptively simple.

In any system, a surprisingly small number of things often determine what the whole system can achieve.

1
Find what matters most.
2
Understand why it matters.
3
Change what needs changing.
4
Then see what happens.

Of course, real life is rarely quite that tidy.

People disagree.
Objectives conflict.
Unintended consequences appear.
Yesterday’s solution becomes tomorrow’s problem.

That’s why we need more than slogans.

We need ways to test our explanations against reality.
Ways to distinguish symptoms from causes.
Ways to uncover the assumptions keeping a conflict alive.
And ways to make progress without requiring everyone to agree about everything first.

We don’t believe everyone needs to learn the vocabulary of the Theory of Constraints.

We believe more people could benefit from experiencing what its thinking tools make possible.

The tools matter. But what people can accomplish with them matters more.

VI.

Five questions that could change quite a lot

Better thinking often begins with surprisingly ordinary questions.

1
What are we actually trying to achieve?

An embarrassingly useful question, especially in organisations that have become extremely busy.

2
What’s stopping us?

Not everything that’s wrong. The things that genuinely limit progress.

3
Why does that happen?

And why does that happen? Keep going until the explanation becomes useful.

4
What are we assuming?

Some of our most formidable obstacles turn out to be beliefs masquerading as facts.

5
What would change our minds?

Because being certain feels wonderful, but discovering you were mistaken can be considerably more valuable.

None of these questions requires a PhD.

They do, however, require something that can be remarkably difficult to find.

The willingness to think together.

Explore the Questions

VII.

A movement for people who suspect there must be a better way

You don’t have to be an expert.

In fact, it may help if you aren’t.

Reason Commons is for people who have ever looked at an established way of doing things and thought:

Surely this can’t be the best we can do?

EDUCATORS
It’s for educators who want children to think rather than merely repeat.
LEADERS
For leaders who suspect their organisations contain more untapped intelligence than their consultants.
ENTREPRENEURS
For entrepreneurs who know the obvious solution is not always the right one.
COMMUNITIES
For communities tired of arguments that generate heat but no light.
PRACTITIONERS
For practitioners who have discovered powerful thinking tools and wonder why more people haven’t encountered them.
ANYONE
And for anyone who believes that disagreement needn’t end in division.
You don’t need permission.
You don’t need a qualification.
You don’t even need to agree with us.

Actually, disagreement could be rather useful.

You just need to be willing to question what seems obvious.

Join the Commons

VIII.

What happens here?

Less intellectual theatre. More useful thinking.

Explore

Discover deceptively simple ideas that change how you see problems.

Practise

Learn to use questions, reasoning tools and experiments on situations that actually matter to you.

Gather

Bring people together around shared challenges, even when they start with different opinions.

Contribute

Share questions, discoveries, stories, tools and explanations that others can learn from.

Spread

Help make better reasoning an everyday human capability, rather than a specialist occupation.

The ambition isn’t to build an audience that admires good thinking.

It’s to build a commons in which people practise it.

IX.
OUR MANIFESTO

We have enough people trying to sound clever.

We could do with more people trying to understand.

We believe a question can be more valuable than an answer.

That disagreement is not necessarily a sign of stupidity.
That complexity is sometimes real, but sometimes merely a symptom of poor explanation.
That local improvements can make the whole worse.
That incentives matter.
That assumptions deserve examination.
That evidence matters more than elegance.
That the purpose of reasoning is not to win arguments, but to make progress.
And that no one has a monopoly on common sense.

Especially us.

Reason Commons is not a movement to tell the world what to think.

It’s a movement to help us think better together.

X.
THE INVITATION

The world probably doesn’t need another methodology.

It might, however, benefit from a renaissance.

A renaissance in curiosity.
In cause and effect.
In intellectual humility.
In the rather unfashionable belief that people with different perspectives can work together to discover something neither could see alone.
And in the possibility that many of our most frustrating problems might become easier to solve once we stop treating their symptoms as their causes.

It begins with a question.

Not a course.
Not a certification.
Not a 147-slide presentation.

Just a question.

What if there’s a better way to think about this?

Welcome to Reason Commons.

A Renaissance of Common Sense.

Reason Commons
The example
For funders
When the same question keeps coming back, check the “because”

It’s on the agenda again. Everyone has reasons, some of them good. Reason Commons helps you set them out one claim at a time and find the one worth testing before you commit.

Talk as usual; one of you types. An AI assistant records who said what, what’s accepted for now and what’s disputed. Changing your mind about one claim becomes a step forward with your name on it.

Suggested
donation £2

A FICTIONAL EXAMPLE

Why are fewer people coming to Thursday lunch?

In October, a volunteer kitchen’s free Thursday lunch gained a sign: “Suggested donation £2.” Three volunteers discuss the falling numbers again; Rosa types.

STEP THROUGH
1 · Rosa
2 · Tom
3 · Jo
4 · Next question
Show all

Showing every step.

An illustration of the record the skill keeps, not its interface.

THE CONVERSATION

Rosa
who keeps the sign-in sheet

“The sheets say we served about 40 lunches. This autumn it’s nearer 25.”

Tom
who cooks

“It’s because of the donation sign. People see it and turn round. Make lunch free again and they’ll come back.”

Assistant

“That assumes the fall came after the sign. Did it?”

Jo
the treasurer

“Maybe not. I think numbers fell the week before the sign, when the toddler group moved to Fridays. Lots of those parents stayed for lunch.”

All three say Rosa’s numbers are right; nobody endorses either explanation.

THE RECORD

Accepted for now
Proposed
Disputed
ROSA’S OBSERVATION
Accepted for now by Rosa, Tom and Jo

Thursday lunches fell from about 40 to about 25 this autumn.

Source: sign-in sheets.

TOM’S EXPLANATION
Proposed

People see the £2 donation sign and turn round.

TOM’S CONNECTION
Proposed, now disputed by Jo
EXAMINE THIS

The sign caused the fall.

ASSUMPTION · PROPOSED BY THE ASSISTANT

The fall came after the sign.

JO’S OBJECTION · OPEN

“I think numbers fell the week before the sign.”

JO’S EXPLANATION
Proposed

The toddler group’s move to Fridays took regular guests with it.

JO’S CONNECTION
Proposed

The move contributed to the fall.

TOM’S POSSIBLE ACTION
Proposed

Make lunch free again.

Tom expects people back. Rests on his explanation.

Her objection makes timing the next question: an hour with the sheets, before anyone decides about money.

NEXT QUESTION
suggested by the assistant

Which week did numbers fall, and whose names disappeared?

The sign’s week, across all kinds of guests
Tom’s connection survives this check, pointing to a month without the sign before scrapping the donation.
The week before, mostly toddler-group parents
Tom’s connection fails on timing, so his action needs rethinking, starting with the toddler group.
A mix, or neither
Ask regulars who stopped coming what changed.
STILL OPEN
Jo’s objection
Both explanations
The donation decision

“Accepted for now” means the group will build on Rosa’s count, not that it’s proven; the sheets are the evidence. If the sheets contradict a claim, its author can narrow it under their own name.

The thinking is yours. The paperwork needn’t be.

Examining a reason still takes effort: fetching the sheets, sitting with an objection, admitting “I might be wrong here.” Reason Commons handles the clerical work: clear wording that keeps each “I think”, who said what, objections pinned to what they challenge, open questions saved for next time, whoever runs it.

No method to learn: a number, a memory of which week, an objection or a question all count.

Where it stands today

Reason Commons is a skill for an AI assistant. You work in conversation; the assistant keeps a structured plain-text record, sketched in the cards above, and scripts check it, draw diagrams and snapshot accepted changes.

One person drives and saves each session, so it isn’t for editing together at once. The scripts check consistency, not truth. Nothing yet shows that groups decide better with it.

Still to build and test:

Automatic prediction follow-up
Tracing everything a failed assumption affects
Ranking review by stakes
Telling independent support from repetition
Reliable transfer between tools
Exchange between groups, keeping acceptance decisions local
Bring your own Thursday-lunch question

Every group has one. Before your next meeting, write down what you’ve seen, the explanation, the action it points to and the assumption joining them. Then find the quickest check that could change your mind.

Register your group’s interest
[Sign-up route to be confirmed]
WHAT YOU’VE SEEN
THE EXPLANATION
THE ACTION IT POINTS TO
THE ASSUMPTION JOINING THEM
THE QUICKEST CHECK THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR MIND
For public funders: what support would test

Reasons vanish when a coordinator leaves or a chat scrolls away. If reasons, dissent and lessons outlasted meetings, successors and neighbouring groups could build on them. Public support would fund a small, facilitated pilot to test that:

Observed sessions

→ findings

Can newcomers contribute, and tell proposals, endorsements and objections apart?

Handover comparison

→ evaluation method

Can a new coordinator recover reasons and the minority objection faster and more accurately than from notes or chat?

Revision and transfer trials

→ documented format

Do claims keep their history, meaning and attribution when revised or moved elsewhere?

Follow-up where feasible

→ an outcome-review prompt and learning materials

Does comparing expectations like Tom’s with outcomes change what groups try next?

Satisfaction and participation can’t settle it.

WHAT WOULD COUNT AGAINST US

Reasons recovered no better from the record than from existing notes, meaning capture and presentation need redesign.

We propose to publish all of it, negative results included.

If you fund public-interest work, help us test whether reasons outlast meetings.

Discuss the pilot
[Contact route to be confirmed]

Reason Commons
Reason Commons

A better way to think together — and to act on it.

Structure the thinking as trees — a tree of change, and a tree of action — with every claim and every step still connected to the goal it serves. Let ordinary discussion attach where it belongs, and let AI keep the tree current. The point is that our thinking should accumulate.

READ THE SERIES
SEE IT WORKING

There's no app to log into yet — a way of thinking, and enough built around it to judge whether it's worth adopting.

On the questions that matter most, we generate plenty of heat and not much light. There is real discussion — on the forum, in long documents, in calls — but it repeats, it scatters, and it doesn't build; you can't point at a 200,000-word strategy and improve one sentence of it. We never build the cathedral, we just make a bigger mess. Trees are a way out: break a goal into the parts it actually rests on, so the whole and the parts stay connected and you can see how a single step — or a single objection — bears on what you're trying to do. Then the hard part, getting freeform discussion connected back to the tree without anyone doing tedious filing. It has to be close to effortless or it won't happen, and AI is what makes that possible now.

The idea

Break a goal, or a claim, into the parts it rests on — a tree of change, and a tree of action — with the whole and the parts kept connected.

The AI tooling we're building

AI drafts the trees from what you already have, and folds ongoing discussion back in — so it enriches the conversation and improves the tree at the same time.

See it working

The four steps end to end — claim, tree, sources, evidence — on a worked toy example.

Grounded in the Logical Thinking Process

A rigorous method from the Theory of Constraints, forty years in the making — it came out of industry, but it applies almost anywhere. We use its rigour and drop its vocabulary.

Start here — the three-part series

The way in is a short scrolling series: why fixes don't stick, why reasoning has to be made visible, and the forty-year-old method that connects them. Then watch the method meet a real movement's strategy in The Forum Doesn't Remember. Full contents on the series page.

DEMOS & EXPERIMENTS — ROUGH, UNFINISHED, ILLUSTRATIVE

DEMO

The four-step vision as an animated walk-through.

PROTOTYPE

A read-only viewer over a full LTP analysis of one organisation's goals and constraints.

EXPERIMENT

Turning a room's scattered goals into one tree everyone can sign off on.

TALK
A talk that performs the method

Five acts; the audience experiences the process before hearing its name.

The method underneath

The rigour comes from the Logical Thinking Process (LTP), part of the Theory of Constraints — a way of laying out a goal, the things blocking it, and the change that gets past them. Our Guide is a plain-language introduction, with a reading list if you want the books.

About

Reason Commons is a collaboration between Rufus Pollock and David Joseph. It has three strands: building the AI tooling; working with communities that already reason hard in public — AI governance, effective altruism, climate; and using Second Renaissance as a living laboratory. Rufus's thread: issue trees and structured problem-framing, a tool he wanted for more than ten years. David's thread: "Abductio," a proposition-decomposition process inside his Promise Protocol framework. More about the project and the people →
